What's the single best resource to learn how to build PCs? I'd like to build a nice one for myself at least once...

I read a book which I think was called "How to Build and Repair PC's." It was written by a computer diagnostics technician, and stressed a testing and diagnostics approach to building and repair. After that I started doing it, and the rest came from there. You inevitably learn more as you go.

Anyways - I think that book is out of print now - can't seem to find it anywhere, and it would be very dated by today's standards - but it looked not unlike something like this:

 

Upgrading and Repairing PCs (22nd Edition) 22nd Edition by Scott Mueller (Author)

 

At the time there was no school that taught this knowledge - you either acquired it through such a book, or by working for someone who did know it.

If you are going to build then you need to know what the actual parts are, what they do, and how they fit together. Do it wrong and you can fry the equipment - which is expensive. Definitely read one, or more, of these books before you begin. It should save you a lot of grief. Even with this knowledge, it is perhaps best to get the help of an experienced tech to walk you through it at least once, to cover the finer points as you go.

 

All computers are the same.

The most important rule to know is this: If all of the parts are all working, and you have plugged them all in correctly, then when you turn on the computer, it WILL work.

So if it is not working, either a part is broken, or not plugged in right. This is true 100% of the time. Parts also include your source of power.

 

Also - these days there are excellent online tutorials - blogs, videos, etc, a vast quantity of information specifically on building, and diagnostic repair. There are probably several videos of building from start to finish - you should still read the book first - it helps to have an awareness of the concepts they are referring to.

Let me give you a small example to emphasize this point - you know how many internet pics are formatted using the jpeg standard - this standard is actually established by committee - to lay down the rules of a common format for jpeg - so that any independent company can produce their software such as it will be compatible with images produced by some other company's software. Such standards are the bread and butter of nearly everything in the mainstream computer world - some are open standards, some are proprietary property, some are secret company knowledge.

Anyways - the same thing happens in computer hardware. The IEEE (international engineering rules committees) establish common factors in the hardware world - everything from electrical compatibility, to the shapes of computer cases - Computer cases follow what is known as form factors - and you need to buy the right types of parts for the right cases if you want everything to fit. That is an example of the types of knowledge covered in the books that can be overlooked in an online video. It is essential knowledge you need to have.

 

At the risk of being overly long winded you should also be aware of the knowledge you really want to pursue first. When I say the word house - you know what a house is. You know all of the common elements of what makes up a house. All houses are the same. Yet, the house you see is not the same as the house I see. You and I can talk all day about houses, because we both understand the common basics of what a house is, and what it is not. This is the same knowledge you need when it comes to computers and their architecture. They are all the same, even as they are all different. Before you can understand the differences, you need to be firmly grounded in the similarities. Then you will be off to an excellent start.
